newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sega slashes profit outlook on US, inventory woes.
newsitem.headline: Sega slashes profit outlook on US, inventory woes.

text.p: Japanese game maker Sega Enterprises Ltd slashed its annual profits forecast on Friday due to problems with accumulated supplies of outdated gameplayers and losses at its U.S. subsidiary.

Sega said it would swallow a substantial special loss in the current business year, which ends in March, to tackle the woes at U.S. unit Sega of America and to dispose of worldwide inventories of old-style 16-bit game players.

As a result of the anticipated 23 billion yen ($200 million) special loss, the firm cut its forecast for net parent profits for 1996/97 by around two-thirds to 5.31 billion yen ($46.1 million) from a November forecast of 16 billion yen ($139 million).
It also cut its forecast for group profit in the same period by almost half, to 5.3 billion yen ($46.0 million) from the previously forecast 10 billion yen ($86.9 million).

"Now that we know our sales in the Christmas shopping season, we will wipe out worldwide inventories of 16-bit machine-related products, worth about seven billion yen ($60.8 million)," Sega said in a statement.
The focus of the home videogame market is rapidly shifting from 16-bit players to the new-generation 32-bit machines.
Sega, which has been encountering stiff competition from rivals such as Sony and Nintendo, did not say how well its products had fare during the Christmas shopping season.

Disposal of inventories is expected to hurt the earnings of Sega of America, which holds about three billion yen ($26.0 million) worth of the seven billion yen ($60.8 million) in inventories targeted for disposal, Sega managing director Shunichi Nakamura told a news conference. Other unwanted inventories are in Europe and Japan.
Sega said it would either sell the unwanted products at a discount or scrap them.
The U.S. unit is already suffering accumulated losses of $215.5 million and Sega will use the extraordinary loss to erase the losses, Nakamura said.
"By erasing the unit's losses, we can get rid of obstacles in our Sega Saturn strategies," Nakamura said.
The Sega Saturn is its 32-bit videogame model.
Industry analysts said Sega has had a setback in the domestic market due to offensives by rival Sony's 32-bit PlayStation and Nintendo's cutting-edge 64-bit game player Nintendo 64.

A media report predicting Sega's earnings revision -- which was formally announced after Tokyo market closed -- pushed the company's share price down on Friday, causing the Tokyo Stock Exchange to suspend trading in the share for the rest of the day. Sega shares closed 50 yen lower at 4,050 yen ($35).
Shares in Japanese information service company CSK, which is Sega's largest shareholder, also fell sharply following the Sega suspension. ($1=115 yen)
